facts.statement: The study analyzed brain scans from more than 500 healthy young people to look at how the signal difference between gray and white matter changes with age.
facts.subject: humans

facts.statement: The difference in signal intensity at the boundary between gray and white matter increased as the participants got older.
facts.subject: humans

facts.statement: As age increased, the thickness of the brain's outer layer decreased at a steady rate, while the degree of folding decreased in a curved pattern.
facts.subject: humans

facts.statement: When the researchers adjusted for the signal difference at the tissue boundary, the link between age and the measured brain features became weaker.
facts.subject: humans

facts.statement: The amount of white matter in the brain was linked to the signal contrast, the thickness of the cortex, and the level of folding.
facts.subject: humans

facts.statement: Even after considering the signal difference, the relationship between age and the brain's thickness and folding was still statistically present.
facts.subject: humans

facts.statement: The results suggest that researchers need to consider this signal difference when studying how the brain changes during development.
facts.subject: humans
